[1,i] The Discourse on the Lion’s Roar of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna-siṃhanāda-sūtra) Chapter One: On the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma (Dharmacakra-pravartana-parivarta) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, you should now proclaim the Mahāyāna Sūtra called ‘The Lion’s Roar. Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and said to him: “Blessed One, what is the name of this Mahāyāna sūtra? And how should it be upheld? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, this Mahāyāna sūtra is named ‘The Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata. It should be upheld by this name. At that moment, the venerable Ānanda, having received this instruction from the Blessed One, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed. He then went to the assembly hall where the great bodhisattvas were gathered. Having arrived, he addressed the great bodhisattva Maitreya: “O son of noble family, the Blessed One has commanded me to proclaim the Mahāyāna sūtra called ‘The Lion’s Roar. O son of noble family, you should listen attentively and bear it well in mind; I shall now explain it for you. Then the great bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Ānanda, please speak; we shall listen with single-minded attention. The venerable Ānanda then spoke these verses: “O you who possess the ten powers, the peerless teacher, The one who has transcended all worlds, the supreme among men— I now wish to ask about the profound meaning of the Dharma. May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, grant me the opportunity. Having spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and condition for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world? What is the cause and condition for the turning of the wheel of the Dharma? What is the cause and condition for the existence of the Mahāyāna? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, the cause and condition for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is the exhaustion of all afflictions and the realization of unconditioned wisdom. The cause and condition for the turning of the wheel of the Dharma is the manifestation of the path of liberation for sentient beings. The cause and condition for the existence of the Mahāyāna is the great vow to bring all beings to ultimate nirvāṇa. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of dharmas that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, the Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata regarding the emptiness of all phenomena. Second, the Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata regarding the signlessness of all phenomena. Third, the Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata regarding the wishlessness of all phenomena. Fourth, the Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata regarding the non-arising of all phenomena. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of fearless proclamations that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, the fearless proclamation that ‘I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Second, the fearless proclamation that ‘I have exhausted all outflows and am free from all defilements. Third, the fearless proclamation that ‘I teach the Dharma that leads to the cessation of suffering. Fourth, the fearless proclamation that ‘I have no equal in the world, nor is there anyone who can surpass me. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of invincibility that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, invincibility in the knowledge of the past. Second, invincibility in the knowledge of the future. Third, invincibility in the knowledge of the present. Fourth, invincibility in the knowledge of the extinction of all outflows. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of sovereignty that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, sovereignty over the lifespan. Second, sovereignty over the mind. Third, sovereignty over necessities. Fourth, sovereignty over the Dharma. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of unimpededness that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, unimpededness in the knowledge of all things. Second, unimpededness in the knowledge of all words. Third, unimpededness in the knowledge of all meanings. Fourth, unimpededness in the knowledge of all eloquence. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of purity that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, purity of body. Second, purity of speech. Third, purity of mind. Fourth, purity of wisdom. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of mastery that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, mastery over the realm of desire. Second, mastery over the realm of form. Third, mastery over the formless realm. Fourth, mastery over the realm of nirvāṇa. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of protection that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, protecting all sentient beings from fear. Second, protecting the true Dharma. Third, protecting the Sangha. Fourth, protecting the precepts. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of light that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, the light of wisdom that dispels the darkness of ignorance. Second, the light of compassion that brings warmth to the cold of suffering. Third, the light of merit that illuminates the path of virtue. Fourth, the light of Dharma that reveals the truth of reality. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of power that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, the power of faith. Second, the power of vigor. Third, the power of mindfulness. Fourth, the power of wisdom. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of fearlessness that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, fearlessness in preaching the Dharma. Second, fearlessness in answering difficult questions. Third, fearlessness in subduing adversaries. Fourth, fearlessness in manifesting miraculous powers. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of equanimity that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, equanimity toward gain and loss. Second, equanimity toward praise and blame. Third, equanimity toward pleasure and pain. Fourth, equanimity toward fame and insignificance. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of non-retrogression that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, non-retrogression in the path of seeing. Second, non-retrogression in the path of cultivation. Third, non-retrogression in the path of no-more-learning. Fourth, non-retrogression in the path of the extinction of outflows. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of unshakeability that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, unshakeability by worldly dharmas. Second, unshakeability by Mara. Third, unshakeability by heterodox teachers. Fourth, unshakeability by the power of karma. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of non-duality that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? First, the non-duality of subject and object. Second, the non-duality of self and other. Third, the non-duality of birth and death and nirvāṇa. Fourth, the non-duality of samsara and enlightenment. “Moreover, Ānanda, there are four kinds of inconceivability that constitute the Lion’s Roar of a Tathāgata. What are the four? Human beings engage in means only with a purpose in view; therefore, the authors of treatises first demonstrate the purpose of their work. In this context, the primary purpose (*svataḥ-prayojana*) consists of pleasure, its enjoyment, and the absence of pain. Its essential nature (*tattva*) is being the object of a desire that is not dependent on another desire; it is not, however, "being a purpose while not producing another purpose," because this would fail to include pleasure that acts as a cause by being the object of the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of pleasure itself. Secondary purpose (*gauṇa-prayojana*), such as eating and so forth, is the object of a desire dependent on another desire, since the desire for it arises only through the recollection of a result in the form of pleasure and the like. Just as heaven is a primary purpose due to its nature as pleasure unmixed with pain, so too liberation (*apavarga*), which consists in the absolute cessation of suffering, is a primary purpose in its own right, being the fruit of treatises such as *Ānvīkṣikī*.

The proof for liberation (*mukti*) is as follows: suffering, or Devadatta’s suffering, subsists in a destruction that is not co-temporal with its own substrate, because it is a mere effect, or because it is a continuum (*santati*), like the nature of a lamp. Being a continuum means subsisting in all effects belonging to different times. Furthermore, the Vedic scripture, “The Self is to be known; he does not return again,” is also a proof. “He returns” means he becomes embodied. Nor can it be argued that liberation, being of the aforementioned nature, cannot be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it is opposed to pleasure; for even though it is necessarily accompanied by the absence of pleasure, there is no obstacle to the arising of desire for it—whether characterized simply as the absence of suffering, or as such an absence specified by its absoluteness, or as such an absence specified by both. Nor should it be said that because it is necessarily accompanied by the absence of pleasure, aversion arises toward it and thus desire is impossible; for that which is an intrinsic goal (*svataḥ-puruṣārtha*) is unfit to be an object of aversion. If it is objected: “Since the means to liberation, such as the practice of yoga, brings about the cessation of pleasure by means of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which destroys merit (*dharma*) and so forth, aversion toward these means may arise; thus, activity on the part of those who possess discernment would be untenable. [The reply is: For sensualists who possess an intense attachment to pleasures, an intense aversion toward the absence of pleasure arises, and consequently they do not engage in the means to liberation at all. As the author of the *Maṇi* has stated: “Therefore, the undiscerning, desiring only pleasure, aim for a pleasure permeated by much more suffering and, thinking ‘Let my head go if it must go,’ they engage in the wives of others and the like.”

Those who speak thus are not qualified for this [path]. However, those who possess discernment (*vivekin*)—who, in this wilderness of *saṃsāra*, consider how many are the days of suffering and how few the fireflies of pleasure, and who regard this [world] as being like the shadow cast by the expanded hood of an angry serpent, and who desire to abandon even pleasure—they are the ones qualified for this. For the discerning, because pleasure is permeated by much greater suffering, there is no intense attachment (*utkaṭarāga*) toward it; and since there is no such attachment, there is likewise no intense aversion (*utkaṭadveṣa*). Since it is precisely the status of being a means to an object of intense aversion that constitutes an obstacle to engagement, there is no logical impossibility of engaging in the means to liberation (*mokṣa*). Even regarding heaven, because it is permeated by suffering born of the fear of falling and because it is perishable, the discerning do not have intense attachment toward it. The intensity of attachment and aversion is a specific type of mental state (*jāti-viśeṣa*) to be inferred from the resulting engagement or withdrawal. The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) governing these is non-uniform (*ananugata*), consisting of various specific cognitions and so forth; for even when the cognition that [pleasure] is permeated by much suffering is equal, intense attachment arises in those who experience pleasure while intense aversion arises in those who lack it, whereas neither arises in the discerning. If it is argued that, as stated in [12.i], the knowledge of liberation is not possible, we say no. For activity does not proceed with the aim, "May I know the absence of suffering"; rather, with the aim, "May suffering not be mine," those whose bodies are shattered by manifold sufferings are seen to engage in death itself for the sake of the absence of suffering, quite spontaneously.

Now, the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanivṛtti*) is the absence of suffering in the form of its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), and not its antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) or absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), because these two are eternal and thus cannot be produced. Furthermore, since destruction is possible through the very specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that arises immediately [after the final moment], knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would have no utility [in producing it]. If it is argued: "The state of being liberation (*apavarga*), defined as the destruction of suffering qualified by 'absolute-ness'—which consists in not being co-temporal with the antecedent absence of suffering residing in the same locus—cannot be established by any other cause independent of the knowledge of reality," even so, such a property cannot possibly be the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the effecthood (*kāryatā*) produced by the knowledge of reality. This is because at the stage of the destruction of the final suffering, there is an absence of the cause—demerit (*adharma*) which generates suffering—in the self possessing that [destruction]; thus, due to the non-arising of further suffering, the property of "not being co-temporal with suffering residing in the same locus" is established by the force of circumstances alone (*arthavaśāt*). Moreover, a property seized by a "collision of facts" (*arthasamāja*) cannot serve as a delimitor of effecthood. Otherwise, properties such as "the destruction of suffering not co-temporal with the suffering of another person" would absurdly result in being delimiters of effecthood for some cause. This is not so. For in a case of a "collision of facts," the absence of a proving factor (*sādhaka*) is indeed the subverter of [a property’s] status as a delimitor of effecthood. However, there is no subversion here, as the causality of the knowledge of reality toward that which is delimited by the aforementioned liberation is attested by scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and so forth. Or, even if there were no causality toward that which is delimited by such liberation, the knowledge of reality remains nonetheless an indispensable *prayojaka* (indirect cause) for that which is so delimited. Without the knowledge of reality, the severance of the stream of sins is impossible, and consequently, the persistence of suffering is necessary; thus, the destruction of suffering could not be established as "not co-temporal with suffering. Whatever, without which a property delimited by something else cannot be established, is precisely the *prayojaka* of that [delimited thing]. And *prayojakatva* is a particular kind of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*). Since the cognition of being an *iṣṭaprayojaka* (an indirect cause of what is desired) is itself the cause of the desire for a means, the desire for the knowledge of reality is established by the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*). Scriptural passages such as "He moves about completely liberated from suffering" and "Neither pleasure nor pain touches the bodiless one who dwells [there]" indicate that the absolute liberation from suffering of those possessing the knowledge of reality refers precisely to the fact that [such knowledge] is the *prayojaka* of liberation.

As for the view that liberation is simply the non-arising of suffering, and that although it is unproduced because it consists of a prior negation (*prāgabhāva*), it is nonetheless achievable through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and other means: this is because the cognition of a means as being conducive to security (*kṣema*) alone is what motivates action. This is observed from the fact that people engage in Vedic rites such as expiatory ceremonies (*prāyaścitta*) with the aim "may suffering not be mine," and in worldly acts such as removing a thorn from the foot. The nature of a means conducive to security consists in the preservation of what has been acquired—that is, the maintenance of the existence of what is already established at a subsequent time. Even for a prior negation, its connection to successive moments is maintained by its opposition to the production of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). And since the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) is the cause for destroying demerit (*adharma*), which is the seed of suffering, and is thus opposed to the arising of suffering, it is the Prābhākaras’ position that the prior negation of suffering is something to be achieved (*sādhya*) by that knowledge.

[17,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you think that the Tathāgata perceives, by means of the Buddha-eye, even a single dharma that has been taught? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not even a single dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because there is no dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata that he is called ‘Tathāgata. Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone were to say, ‘The Tathāgata has taught a dharma,’ they would speak falsely, Subhūti, they would be misrepresenting me with what is untrue. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, is there any dharma at all that has been taught by the Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, there is not even a minute particle of a dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if there is not even a minute particle of a dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata, how then does one come to know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Even the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of unqualified suffering, when connected with a subsequent time, is common to the state of *saṃsāra*; therefore, liberation must be defined as that very [non-existence] qualified by the destruction of a suffering that is not co-temporal with any suffering residing in its own locus. Yet such a thing is unestablished, because for one who is liberated, due to the non-arising of suffering, the prior non-existence of that [future] suffering does not exist at the time of liberation. This is because only a future [suffering] can be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a prior non-existence. Furthermore, the desire "May I have no suffering" has as its object only the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of suffering qualified by its connection with successive points in time; even though this [absolute non-existence] is eternal, its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) remains intact, just like a prior non-existence. It may be easily stated that liberation is the absolute non-existence of suffering qualified by the absence of the prior non-existence of suffering, so that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to states such as deep sleep, because the qualifier is absent then. Now, if it is argued: "Just as in the case of bathing in a distant lake—which is to be accomplished through means such as [first] cooling the heat [of distress] characterized by specific qualifications like being preceded by those means—even if the result (the cooling of heat) is achieved without effort through [other means like] a mental state (*vṛtti*), once one perceives that the essential result (the cooling of heat) can be achieved through rain and the like, one does not engage in bathing in the distant lake because of a powerful aversion toward the resulting labor; likewise, since the mere cessation of suffering as a result can be achieved through easy means, even if one desires liberation in the form of the absolute cessation of suffering, engagement in the practice of yoga—which involves immense labor—is untenable. This is not so. Just as, even when one perceives that mere pleasure can be obtained by easy means, people still engage in sacrifices and the like—though they are accomplished only through great expenditure of wealth and effort—if they desire heaven in the form of pleasure unmixed with suffering, because a powerful passion (*rāga*) is possible when the qualification of being "unmixed with suffering" is prioritized, and thus a powerful aversion does not arise toward the great expenditure of wealth and effort; likewise, since a powerful passion is experienced when the qualification of "absoluteness" (*ātyantikatva*) is prioritized, engagement in the means to liberation—which involves immense labor—is possible due to the desire for that result as qualified by it. However, in the case of the result of the cooling of heat qualified by being preceded by bathing in a lake, there is an absence of intense passion because that qualification is not a determinant of desirability (*upādeyatānavacchedaka*); hence, engagement in bathing in the lake in the aforementioned instance is inappropriate.

Some, however, considering that the destruction of suffering can occur through other means alone and thus does not necessarily result from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), accept that liberation (*mokṣa*) consists solely in the absolute destruction of the demerit (*durita*) which is the seed of suffering. Its absoluteness (*ātyantikatva*) is defined as being non-co-temporal with any demerit residing in the same locus (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*). This qualification is included to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the destruction of demerit produced by experience (*bhoga*) or by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). It should not be argued: "Even when the knowledge of reality has arisen, the actions (*karma*) that have already begun to produce the current body are exhausted only through experience; for this very reason, even those who possess the knowledge of reality, such as Nārada and others, engage in the means for pleasure and desist from the means for pain. Consequently, the cessation of demerit produced by the knowledge of reality is co-temporal with such demerit, and thus the aforementioned form of absoluteness cannot be established. This is not so, because even when the knowledge of reality has arisen, it is accepted that the destruction of other demerits occurs through a subsequent instance of the knowledge of reality only after the actions that initiated the current body have been exhausted through experience. It is precisely that [subsequent] destruction which, being absolute, constitutes liberation. Nor should it be argued: "While such [initiating] actions still exist, why would other actions not be destroyed by the power of the knowledge of reality, which is the destroyer? For we accept that the specific universal (*jāti*) which delimits the capacity to destroy demerit resides only in the *final* knowledge of reality (*caramatattvajñāna*). Furthermore, it should not be argued: "If all demerit is destroyed by the knowledge of reality, its absoluteness—in the sense of being non-co-temporal with demerit in its own locus—is established automatically by the force of the facts; therefore, the definition of liberation as 'the destruction of demerit that is non-co-temporal with the demerit of another person' cannot serve as the delimitor of the state of being produced by the knowledge of reality. Moreover, since no specific universal can be postulated among demerits as the delimitor of their being destroyed by the knowledge of reality (due to the risk of confusion with universals delimiting the production of sins like cow-slaughter), and since even the unqualified destruction of demerit cannot be the delimitor of being produced by the knowledge of reality (because of the deviation found in the destruction of demerit caused by experience, etc.), how can the knowledge of reality be a cause for such liberation? This objection is invalid. Since the destruction of demerit occurs through the knowledge of reality even without the causal complex consisting of experience and the like, its causality there is necessary. Out of necessity, it is established that the property delimited by absoluteness is indeed the delimitor of the state of being produced by the knowledge of reality. The lack of evidence is the only obstacle to accepting the destruction of demerit—qualified by being non-co-temporal with the demerit of another person—as the delimitor of the state of being produced. Now, one might argue that the causality of the knowledge of reality regarding the destruction of demerit is unproven, because it is accepted that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is destroyed everywhere through experience alone; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with scriptural statements such as "Karma is not exhausted until it has been experienced. Thus, one might argue that the capacity of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) to destroy karma—established by numerous scriptural statements—is indeed difficult to refute. However, this is not so; for, in accordance with the contradiction posed by such statements as "what has not been experienced [does not perish]," the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those passages teaching that knowledge destroys karma must be understood as follows: knowledge destroys those karmas only after swiftly bringing about the experience of all karmas through the production of a plurality of bodies (*kāyavyūha*). Just as fire is the cause of the destruction of fuel and the subsequent ash only through a mediated process, so too is the destruction of karma by knowledge. It is precisely to indicate this that knowledge is described as being like fire. One should not object: "In the statement *mābhuktam* etc., the word 'karma' must be accepted as referring to *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since its primary power (*śakti*) lies only in action (*kriyā*); therefore, if secondary indication is necessary, let it apply to that *adṛṣṭa* which is not destroyed by knowledge and the like. Since the contradiction is resolved by this alone, why postulate that those possessing the knowledge of reality must experience all their karmas? This objection is invalid. For even regarding *adṛṣṭa*, we observe the traditional usage of the word 'karma' from time immemorial; thus, secondary indication in its general form is equivalent to primary power (*śakti*). Furthermore, in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*), it is improper to assume a natural secondary indication in a specific sense. Nor should it be argued that, because in this view the experience of karmas is mandatory, an "unexperienced" (*abhukta*) karma is impossible, and thus the literal meaning of such a statement is untenable. This is because the past participle suffix (*kta*) intends to express the state of having passed away; there is no room for the impossibility of the literal meaning—which is the negation of being the counter-positive of destruction—in a karma that has not yet been qualified by an experience that has passed away relative to its destruction. Even if "experience" (*bhoga*) is a specific kind of perception and "having been experienced" (*bhuktatva*)—defined as being the object of such perception—is not found anywhere in *adṛṣṭa*, nevertheless, what is intended here is simply the "being an object of experience" in the sense of being the substrate of the fruit (*phala*) that is the object of experience. This is because we observe usages such as "merit is experienced" (*puṇyaṃ bhujyate*) just as "pleasure is experienced" (*sukhaṃ bhujyate*), and such a meaning is established by the natural force of language. [Reply: No. By the phrase "even in hundreds of millions of aeons," it is understood that while a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called *bhāvanā* perishes without producing its fruit due to the lapse of time, karma does not. Thus, there is no contradiction in karma being destroyed even by knowledge; otherwise, since expiation (*prāyaścitta*) also destroys karma, the aforementioned scriptural contradiction could not be avoided. Moreover, if expiation did not destroy sin, there would be no motivation to engage in it. Nor can it be argued that expiation destroys sin only by swiftly bringing about experience through the production of a plurality of bodies, thereby making engagement in it logical. For if individual instances of suffering were identical, there would be no distinction between experiencing them immediately or with delay, rendering expiation useless. Furthermore, it is not correct to claim that even for the knowers of reality (*jñānin*), all karmas must necessarily be experienced in order to avoid contradicting the rule "what has been done must necessarily be experienced. This is because there is no experience of karmas for which expiation has been performed; thus, in those cases, the word 'karma' must necessarily refer to those karmas whose destruction is not brought about by factors taught in the Veda. Since the knowledge of reality is itself taught in the Veda as a destroyer, there is no harm in its destroying karma without experience. Nor should one suspect that because the knowledge of reality directly destroys *adṛṣṭa*, there is a lack of universal concomitance (*vyabhicāra*)—where experience occurs in some cases and knowledge in others—making experience an unfitting cause for the destruction of *adṛṣṭa*. This is because the property of "destruction of *adṛṣṭa* qualified by experience" serves as the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) produced by experience, leaving no room for deviation. Otherwise, there would still be deviation in the case of the destruction of *adṛṣṭa* produced by expiation, recitation, and the like. If it is asked: "Since the destruction of vice (*duritanāśa*) is distinct from pleasure and the absence of pain, how can it be an end-in-itself (*svataḥprayojana*)?", the answer is: it is not an end-in-itself in any direct sense, but rather a secondary end (*gauṇaprayojana*) by virtue of being the means to bring about the absence of pain. If it is further asked: "In this way, since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) born of false cognition causes pain through the medium of *adṛṣṭa*, its cessation is also an end of man by virtue of bringing about the absence of pain; why then is the cessation of that impression alone not accepted as liberation (*mokṣa*)?", the answer is: no. For even when the latent impressions have ceased in those who have attained the knowledge of reality, liberation is not admitted until the karmas that have begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha-karma*) are exhausted. As the scripture states: "He remains [in this world] only as long as he is not liberated; then he shall attain oneness (*kaivalya*)"—this indicates that for the knower of reality, the attainment of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) is delayed until the exhaustion of the commenced karmas. Thus they say.

However, for the Ekadaṇḍins and Vedāntins, liberation (*kaivalya*) is simply the removal of such an adjunct (*upādhi*), which constitutes the pure nature of Brahman as it is unconditioned by any adjunct. Such an adjunct is indeed nescience (*avidyā*); therefore, its cessation is itself [liberation]. Although the cessation of nescience lacks intrinsic purpose because suffering is a property of the specific internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—namely, the intellect (*buddhi*)—and that [intellect] is destroyed by the destruction of the nescience associated with one's own kin, it nonetheless possesses an undeniable secondary purpose (*gauṇaprayojanatva*) as the cause for the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, nescience is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) that, though unproduced, is subject to destruction, and its destroyer is the realization of Brahman (*brahmasaṃvedana*). Nor should it be argued that the realization of Brahman is impossible while the veil in the form of nescience exists; for the realization of Brahman is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of Brahman—a transformation of the internal organ known as a "cognitive state" (*vṛtti*)—which has as its fruit the removal of the nescience that veils the object. Transcending delusion and purified, he is called by the sages the "one whose form has passed beyond delusion. He is the Witness; when his body is reflected within the internal organ arising from that [delusion], he is designated as the "knower" (*pramātṛ*). Thus [it is said]: The manifestation (*sphūrti*) of Brahman occurs by its own nature alone, and not from a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), because it is impossible for a reflection of consciousness to exist within the reality that is consciousness itself. By this, the following objection is refuted: "If the self-awareness of Brahman is simply the knowledge of Brahman, and thus Brahman itself—being of the nature of knowledge regarding its own object—is such [a manifestor], then since it exists eternally even during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), it would follow that ignorance (*avidyā*) must be removed even then. For the Tridaṇḍins, however, liberation (*mok�sa*) is the dissolution of the individual self (*jīvātman*) into the Supreme Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-paramātman*). Although there is non-difference between the Supreme Self and the individual self, the individual self exists as such by virtue of being qualified by specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, its distinction from the Supreme Self is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Therefore, liberation consists precisely in the removal of these distinguishing adjuncts, just as the dissolution of the "space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*) into pure space occurs only upon the disappearance of the jar. Since the state of being an individual self belongs only to the self as delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), liberation culminates in the destruction of the subtle body. The subtle body is a collection of the eleven organs and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—namely, the intellect (*mahat*), egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements—which constitute the seeds of the gross body. It is only when the self is qualified by this [subtle body] that it possesses suffering and other attributes; therefore, upon the destruction of the subtle body—which serves as the qualifier—the occurrence of suffering and so forth is no longer possible. In this context, the "qualifier" is either (1) included within the substratum (*āśraya*) through a specific relation called "delimitation" (*avacchedakatva*), or (2) the mere [delimiting] element itself is the substratum, because in either case it is the cause of suffering. Thus, since the removal of that [subtle body] is the cause for the cessation of suffering, its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) remains intact. Even so, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is dependent on *māyā*, ceases only upon the cessation of *māyā*, the cessation of *māyā* is necessary in the state of liberation. In this system, ignorance (*avidyā*) is defined as *māyā*; therefore, in effect, there is no difference.

[40,i] Here, the logicians (*nyāyavidaḥ*) maintain that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*), as there is no means of valid cognition (*māna*) for such; rather, it is simply the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) itself which, by virtue of being opposed to knowledge (*vidyā*) consisting of the realization of reality, is called "ignorance. Although individual instances of the unseen force are beginningless, the traditional teaching that ignorance is beginningless refers to the beginninglessness of its continuum (*pravāha*). Thus, liberation (*mokṣa*) is unimpededly established as either the cessation of that [ignorance] or the cessation of suffering dependent upon it.

As for the claim that when ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases, the intellect (*buddhi*) and its concomitants cease, and consequently suffering—which is their property—ceases, this too does not withstand logical scrutiny. For if the intellect is the substratum (*āśraya*) of pleasure, pain, and so forth, there is no evidence for its destruction. Nor can one accept its destruction merely out of a desire for the absolute eradication of suffering; for even while the intellect exists, the stream of suffering can be interrupted simply through the eradication of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, it is not the case that the total destruction of all *adṛṣṭa* is impossible without the destruction of its substratum; for even while the substratum exists, the destruction of all *adṛṣṭa* is possible through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which has the same locus as that *adṛṣṭa*. Moreover, in your own view, the destruction of ignorance necessarily requires [the destruction of] its cause. Finally, the non-arising of further *adṛṣṭa* in the case of yogis is due to the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like; for even while the intellect and its concomitants exist, *adṛṣṭa* arises, and thus in your view as well, *adṛṣṭa* is caused by latent impressions.

Now, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were a distinct category (*padārthāntara*), let it not be so; rather, let ignorance be either the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) or simply the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by false knowledge. True knowledge (*tattvajñāna*), however, is not the direct cause for the destruction of the unseen; rather, it is the destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*) itself. This is because, since the intellect is the substratum of cognition and the like, true knowledge—as its substratum—possesses the property of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the destruction [of the unseen] through a direct relation. In the case of the unseen, true knowledge exists only through an indirect relation consisting of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); therefore, for it to be the destroyer of that [unseen], there would be a complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting relation of the power of destruction. Nor should it be argued that accepting true knowledge as the destroyer of the unseen through a relation residing in the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is complex, and thus one must accept its causality toward destruction through a direct relation residing in the locus of destruction. For if that were the case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the absence of a restrictive rule. Likewise, in the Nyāya system, there is complexity in postulating a separate causal efficacy for true knowledge in the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Since the destruction of latent impressions is accounted for simply by the destruction of the [intellect]—just as the destruction of the unseen is—the separate causal efficacy of true knowledge need not be admitted. Furthermore, in the destruction of the unseen and so forth, the causality of the destruction of the intellect adds nothing extra, as this is already accounted for by the well-established causality of the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya*) toward the destruction of the dependent (*āśrita*). Thus, if it is argued that liberation (*apavarga*) is simply the disappearance of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of that living self (*jīva*), we say no. For if the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) were beginningless, its destruction would be impossible, since a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) must be produced for the destruction of an entity to occur. If, on the other hand, it has a beginning, then the stream of the unseen—which is a quality of the intellect—would also have a beginning; consequently, there could be no initial diversity of the unseen nor the resulting diversity of effects such as experience. Nor can the diversity of the volition (*kṛti*) that produces the unseen account for the initial state, as the very cause of the initial diversity of volition is difficult to find. Therefore, the unseen must be eternal insofar as it inheres in [the self]; the diversity of experience among persons arises from an beginningless stream of diverse unseen forces. Thus, [the view that liberation is the removal of the intellect's adjunct is not tenable].

[43,i] By this it is shown that the intellect (*buddhi*), known as the "Great One" (*mahat*), is a specific transformation of the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); in that very intellect reside the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), merit, and so forth. The *puruṣas*, however, are of the nature of immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*). Immovability (*kauṭasthya*) consists in not being a substratum for the properties of birth and destruction. Properties such as action and so forth belong to the intellect; they are superimposed upon the *puruṣa* by means of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is a specific transformation of the intellect. As it has been said: "One whose self is deluded by the ego thinks, 'I am the doer.'"

The Sāṅkhya doctrine— that the bondage of persons consists precisely in the application of the intellect (*buddhi*), and that their liberation consists in its dissolution and the resulting absence of its coloring— is refuted.
Because the intellect (*buddhi*) is swallowed up by the conceptual alternatives of being either beginningless or having a beginning, as it has been stated by the Teachers:
"Otherwise, there would be no liberation, or else there would be no transmigratory existence (*asaṃsāra*).
Here, "no transmigratory existence" means the absence of diversity in transmigratory existence.

The Bhaṭṭas, however, maintain that liberation (*apavarga*) is the direct perception of eternal bliss. Nor is eternal bliss lacking in authority, for there exists scriptural evidence such as: "Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is established in liberation. Here, *ānandam* is a Vedic neuter form; the meaning is that the nature of Brahman—which is an attribute of the Self—is "established" (i.e., directly perceived) in liberation, at the time of liberation. Once the existence of such bliss, which is the object of perception at the time of liberation, is established by such evidence, its eternality follows by parsimony (*lāghava*), given the proof of its lack of production and destruction.

[46,i] However, some say that the scriptural text, "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss," teaches the eternity of the self as qualified by bliss; for since it is a general rule that the connection of the qualified entity is intended when there is no subverting evidence, it is improper to abandon it. Thus, they maintain that this very text is the authority for the eternity of the qualifier, bliss.

That is to be questioned; for if that were so, it would follow that eternal knowledge (*nityajñāna*) would also be established [as a property of the self]. Nor is that accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas; rather, it is only for the Vedāntins that such a supreme self, consisting of knowledge and bliss, is established on the strength of the scriptural texts exactly as they are heard. And for them, through syntactic unity with those texts, the phrase "bliss is the nature of Brahman" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo rūpam*) means "bliss is the essential form of Brahman. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "established in liberation" (*mokṣe pratiṣṭhitam*), since the locative case denotes the sense of being the cause (*janakatā*), the meaning is either that it will come to be [as the cause], or—by supplying the word "will be"—that it is the object of the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) which is the cause of liberation in the form of the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*).

Now, one might argue that because of the contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "Indeed, pleasure and pain do not touch the bodiless one who dwells [in liberation]," it is impossible to accept a connection with happiness for the liberated soul (*mukta*). Nor can it be said that, out of fear of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the intent is not to negate each [pleasure and pain] individually, but rather to intend the absence of both; and thus, even if happiness exists, there is no contradiction because the absence of both is present due to the absence of pain. This argument—that the avoidance of sentence-splitting is achieved by taking the passage to mean the absence of an absence delimited by a non-inherently distributed (*avyāsajyavṛtti*) common property—is not sound, for that possibility arises only when "pleasure" and "pain" are expressed by a single word (which they are not). Furthermore, even this does not resolve the issue of semantic inappropriateness (*ayogyatva*). One should not suspect a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the absence of both is due to the absence of pain or the absence of happiness; for the absence of pain is established by scripture, such as, "He moves about completely freed from suffering," and it is that which necessitates the absence of both. To this we reply: the statement "pleasure and pain do not touch [him]" does not convey the mere absence of those two, but rather the absence of the agency of touching on the part of the liberated self, which is the substratum (*anuyogin*) of that pair. The "agency of touching" that substratum refers to being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of a relation having that [pair] as its object. Now, while the counter-correlativity of such a relation exists in the case of "pleasure"—that is, happiness—the absence of that [counter-correlativity] is sublated even in the case of the "bothness" (*ubhayatva*) delimited by the pair, because we do not admit the existence of an absence delimited by a non-inherently distributed property (*vyāsajyavṛttidharma*) in a locus where its counter-correlate is present. Nor should it be argued that the root *spṛś* here means "existence" (*sattā*), so that just as in the sentence "the pot and cloth do not exist" the existence of the absence of both pot and cloth is understood, so too here the existence of the absence of both pleasure and pain is understood. For if that were so, the root would be intransitive, making the accusative "bodiless" (*aśarīram*) unaccountable; moreover, it is impossible to convey the absence of a nominal stem's meaning without a locative case denoting the substratum. This is not so. Out of fear of contradicting scriptures that teach the bliss of liberation, such as "Bliss (*ānanda*)," we accept that although happiness exists in the liberated self, the absence of counter-correlativity to a relation residing in the liberated self belongs to that which is delimited by "bothness," which is not the delimitor of the occurrence of happiness therein. This is necessary because of common usage such as, "Only one goes, not two," which implies that an absence whose substratum is the locus of the counter-correlate must have a substratum-locus determined by a non-inherently distributed property. Alternatively, the meaning of "do not touch" is the absence of counter-correlativity to a relation consisting of origination (*utpatti*). Nor should it be argued that if the root meant a relation of origination, it would be intransitive like *jan* (to be born) and the like. For roots such as *jan* are intransitive precisely because their meaning is a relation having the first moment as its substratum; here, since the meaning of the root is a relation delimited by the first moment, the self can be the object (*karman*) by virtue of being the substratum of that [relation]. Or, the word "pleasure" (*priya*) may refer specifically to produced happiness (*janyasukha*), and thus there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Now, if it is argued that for one who is liberated (*mukta*), the direct realization of bliss is impossible due to the absence of a body as its instrumental cause—and furthermore, if that realization were eternal, there would be no distinction between the liberated and the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*)—we say: no. This is because the body is a cause only with respect to *limited* knowledge (*avacchinna-jñāna*). Since the direct realization of eternal bliss is not limited by a body, its production is possible even without a body. In the Nyāya system, since "producedness" (*janyatva*) must necessarily be included to exclude the eternal knowledge of God (*īśvara*), there is no room for the objection of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) even if "being limited" (*avacchinnatva*) is introduced as the delimitor of the causal relation for being produced by a body. In reality, since the body is a cause for knowledge only through the relation of "delimitorship" (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*), and since the direct realization of eternal bliss is never produced in anything by that relation, such a realization is possible even for one without a body. Nor should it be said that, in this case, there would be unlimited knowledge even at other times without a body; for the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for knowledge that does not involve a body is constituted by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Nor should it be said that if produced knowledge were the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*), then liberation would cease upon the destruction of that knowledge; for they say that even when individual instances of that knowledge cease, the stream of the direct realization of bliss does not cease.

Even in that [Advaita] view, since the absolute liberation from suffering—or the absolute cessation of the demerit (*durita*) that is the cause of suffering—is necessary at the stage of liberation, it is more appropriate for liberation itself to consist in the absolute cessation of suffering and so forth, rather than for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) to be its cause. Furthermore, the postulation of eternal bliss and its direct perception is refuted by the principle of complexity (*gaurava*). In the passage "Bliss is the nature of Brahman" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo rūpam*), the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) refers simply to the absence of suffering; its meaning is that it remains established in liberation once false knowledge along with its latent impressions (*savāsanamithyājñāna*) has ceased, being without further limit. The knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) is the cause of liberation, according to the Śruti: "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon; it is to be realized. To this extent, indeed, is immortality. Here, "to this extent" means that knowledge consisting of hearing and so forth is the cause of immortality—that is, the cause of liberation. The reason for this is that it is the direct realization of the self as distinct from the body, produced by the merit (*dharma*) arising from meditation practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion, according to the yoga-method taught in the Śruti and Smṛti, which is capable of uprooting false knowledge along with its latent impressions. This is because verbal knowledge (derived from scripture, etc. does not obstruct false cognitions such as "I am fair," which are produced by the specific defect of the latent impression of identifying the self with the body, nor does it destroy the latent impressions generated by those [false cognitions]. Hearing and so forth are useful for liberation only through that [realization]. For this very reason, even during the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), although there exists knowledge of the self in the form of verbal cognition denoted by the term "hearing," inference of the self's difference from others based on reasons of dissimilarity taught in the scriptures denoted by the term "reflection," and the desire conjoined with meditation having the same object as that [inference], dependent on the impressions rooted in hearing and so forth denoted by the term "meditation," liberation does not arise. Nor should it be asked: "Even when hearing and so forth exist, why does the direct realization of the true nature of the self not arise now? For that is to be accomplished through a succession of meditations over a long period of time. As it has been said: [The original Sanskrit verse would follow here.]
By means of scripture, inference, and the delight in the practice of meditation,
one who develops wisdom in these three ways attains the supreme yoga.

The "taste for the practice of meditation" (*dhyānābhyāsarasa*) is the desire to remember [the object] repeatedly. By fashioning—that is, accomplishing—the threefold wisdom consisting of the three types of knowledge known as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), one attains the supreme yoga, which is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of the Self; this is the meaning. Even though the Self is taught in scripture to be distinct from the body and so forth, because there is a possibility that such a teaching might be erroneous—due to the suspicion that the scriptural passage may intend a different meaning on account of its contradiction with other scriptural passages already heard—it is not possible to engage in *nididhyāsana* without faith. Therefore, reflection (*manana*) is useful immediately after hearing (*śravaṇa*). When reflection occurs through the ascertainment of the validity of the object established by reasoning, lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) is removed. For this very reason, the study of the systems of logic and atomism (*nyāya-vaiśeṣika*) is useful for liberation.

Some, however, maintain that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of God alone is the cause of liberation (*mokṣa*). Even though He is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), the direct realization of Him is possible through a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) consisting of the merit (*dharma*) born of yoga (*yogaja*). Nor should it be argued that the claim that the realization of God is the cause of liberation lacks scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*), because in passages such as "The Self is to be heard" (*ātmā śrotavyaḥ*), the word "Self" (*ātman*) could possibly refer to the individual soul (*jīvātman*). This is not so, because the passage "I know this supreme Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness," introduces God (*īśvara*), and the subsequent statement "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" teaches that knowledge of Him alone is the cause of liberation. Since these form a single syntactic unit, the word "Self" in "The Self is to be heard" and similar passages must also refer to God. For this very reason:
This practice of logic, which bears the designation of "reflection" (manana) regarding the Lord,
is in fact nothing but meditative worship (upāsanā), following immediately after hearing (śravaṇa).

Thus, the text of the Teacher (*ācārya*) is also consistent. It should not be argued that the direct realization of God (*īśvarasākṣātkāra*) does not remove false knowledge regarding one’s own self by way of being a contrary cognition (*viparītajñāna*), but rather that it is only the direct realization of the reality of one's own self (*svātmatattvasākṣātkāra*) that is the cause of liberation; for the direct realization of God removes false knowledge precisely by destroying the defects in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Even if the direct realization of God does not remove contrary cognition, there is no harm in accepting that it independently destroys the latent impressions produced by false intellect. Since there is a distinction between the relationship of destroyer and destroyed between latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and contrary cognition based on a difference in their objects, one must also postulate the causality of the direct realization of the self—which apprehends the difference from the body—in the destruction of the latent impression of non-difference between the self and the body. Therefore, in the view that the direct realization of God is the destroyer of that [impression], there is no room for the charge of complexity (*gaurava*). Alternatively, let the utility of the direct realization of the reality of one’s own self be for the sake of destroying latent impressions. For this very reason, the text of the Teacher—that "the self alone is to be known in its true nature as the locus (*anuyogin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)"—is consistent. However, the cause of liberation is indeed the direct realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasākṣātkāra*). It should not be argued that since the merit born of yoga (*yogajadharma*) illuminates the entire universe, when the direct realization of the Supreme Self is produced by it, everything would necessarily appear therein. Consequently, the exclusion of objects other than that [Self]—which is understood by the particle *eva* in the phrase "having known Him alone" (*tam eva viditvā*)—would be contradicted in the case of the knowledge of God. How then can such a scriptural passage have God as its purport? [Response: Even in the case of the direct realization of the self, which you accept as the cause of liberation, there is a contradiction in the exclusion of other objects because it has as its object the difference from the body and so forth. Therefore, in our view, the non-conceptual realization of the Supreme Self, which is the cause of liberation, is established as having no other object by postulating that the causal complex for that [realization] acts as a sublater (*pratibandhaka*) of anything else. An interpretation that resolves the issue by transposing the particle *eva* in the phrase "having known Him alone" (*taṃ viditvaiva*) is equally available in both systems. In fact, if the particle *eva* were transposed, it would be redundant; for the statement "there is no other path for going" already excludes anything other than the knowledge of reality within the causal complex for liberation, and from that very statement, the necessity of a knowledge of reality co-located with liberation (prior to it) is obtained. Thus, it is more appropriate that the direct realization of God alone is the cause, since in that case, as explained above, consistency is possible even without transposing the particle *eva*. Now, if it is argued that because of the natural sense of scriptural texts teaching the non-difference of the individual self (*jīvātman*) from the Supreme Self—such as "from whence these beings are born... thou art That, O Śvetaketu"—you must accept that a cognition such as "I am Brahman" is the cause of your liberation, then the contradiction regarding the exclusion of other objects in the knowledge of God (which is the cause of liberation) would remain, and thus you too would necessarily have to transpose the particle *eva*. By this very argument, it is refuted that the particle *eva* does not exclude the state of having other objects in the knowledge of Him (God) which is the cause of liberation; rather, through the understanding of the positive connection (*bhāvānvaya*) regarding the state of being produced by a knowledge qualified by having that [God] as its object in liberation, the particle *eva* excludes the state of being produced by a knowledge of Him qualified by having other objects. Thus, the result is the exclusion of the state of having other objects as being the motivator of liberation. Therefore, even if other things not useful for the direct realization of God must necessarily appear due to the force of the causal complex, there is no harm. On the other hand, in the view where the direct realization of the individual self is the cause, consistency cannot be achieved even by not transposing the particle *eva* in the manner described above; for in that system, the realization of the self is the cause only by virtue of having as its object the difference from others, and thus it is impossible to exclude the state of having other objects as being the motivator of liberation. This is also refuted by the fact that, according to the Nyāya system, the cognition "I am Brahman" is a cause of liberation even when it has as its object the individual self as non-different from Brahman, as it stands in syntactic unity with injunctions for meditation such as "Brahman alone am I, not a transmigrating being. If it is argued that although the knowledge of non-difference between the individual self and Brahman is an error under the theory of the plurality of selves, it does not contradict scripture that such a knowledge is the cause of liberation, we say no. For the intention of the sentence "That Thou Art" (*tat tvam asi*) is that the direct realization of God—the cause of liberation—is accomplished through the repeated practice of yoga consisting of the contemplation of the non-difference of the individual self and Brahman. Thus, they maintain that the literal reading of "having known Him alone" (*tam eva viditvā*) is consistent.

The authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others, however, maintain that in passages such as, "It is not for the sake of the husband’s desire that the husband is dear, but for the sake of one’s own self that the husband is dear," the quality of being "dear"—defined as being an object of affection for the husband, son, and so forth—due to their capacity to produce [pleasure], is stated to be for the sake of the self's pleasure and the like. In this context, the word *ātman* refers exclusively to the individual self (*jīva*), and not to the Lord (*Īśvara*), because the Lord lacks pleasure. Even for those who consider [the self] to be bliss (*ānanda*), since that bliss is admitted to be eternal, it cannot be an objective end (*uddeśya*). Furthermore, in passages such as, "O King, for all beings, one's own self alone is most beloved," it is stated that one's own self alone is dear without qualification. Thus, since the individual self is the subject introduced [at the beginning], the scriptural passage, "The Self, indeed, is to be heard," etc., teaches that hearing and other means regarding one's own self alone are the cause of liberation, and not the Supreme Self. Nor should it be argued: "Let the purport of such scriptures be that the knowledge of the reality of one's own self is useful for the absolute cessation of suffering by way of destroying false cognition, latent impressions, merit, and demerit; even so, the status of the direct realization of the Lord as a distinct cause—established by scriptures such as 'Having known Him alone'—remains unassailable. This is because, once liberation in the form of the absolute departure of suffering and the like is accomplished through the destruction of merit and demerit alone, there is no logical justification for the direct realization of the Supreme Self to be a cause therein. Rather, it is more appropriate to assume that the purport of the scripture "Having known Him alone" lies in its syntactic unity with the injunction for the practice of yoga, whereby the practice of yoga—which consists of the contemplation of the non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman—is useful for liberation by producing the direct realization of one's own self. And in this way, even the transposition of the particle *eva* (alone) does not cause any harm. Since the portion of the text beginning with "There is no other path" can be meaningful as a clarifier of the purport of that *eva*, they say that it is like the portion "none other than Maheśvara Tryambaka" in passages such as "Maheśvara Tryambaka alone, and no other."

In that view, there is an unavoidable contradiction with the literal meaning of such statements as "Yogins perceive that Blessed One who is beyond the senses," which holds that the fruit of the practice of yoga is the direct realization of the Supreme Brahman.

Now, since it is heard many times that even acts such as dying at Kāśī or beholding the face of Puruṣottama (Viṣṇu) are means to liberation, how can there be consistency with statements such as "There is no other path"? Furthermore, how can one establish a unified causal efficacy toward liberation for these various, non-uniform specific cognitions and actions? The causality of grass, fire-sticks, and jewels toward fire is established by the distinctness (*vaijātya*) of their effects, because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). However, in the case of liberation—which is of the nature of a negation—it is impossible to postulate a specific universal (*jāti*). Nor can deviation be avoided by postulating specific universals in the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), such as suffering or sin, and then accepting those [negations] delimited by such universals as being related to their own substrates via the relation of having that as the counter-correlate, or by accepting those very [negations] as the delimiters of the effect-ness; for there would be the undesirable consequence of *saṅkara* (overlapping) with the universals that delimit the effect-ness of cow-slaughter and so forth, which leaves no room for the postulation of [new] universals. Nor should it be said that there is no risk of *saṅkara* because one accepts a plurality of universals delimiting the effect-ness of cow-slaughter and so on; for it is difficult to find a decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*) as to whether that plurality belongs to those [universals] or to the universals that delimit the perishability by true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) and so forth. Likewise, in cases where the scripture teaches optional causality (*vaikalpika-hetutā*), the result is not produced from the combined [factors], because the single ritual application (*ekayoga*) is not performed with both rice and barley together. If cognition and action were causes like grass, fire-sticks, and jewels, then it would follow that liberation would be absent when they are combined. Nor is there consistency in accepting that the combination of cognition and action is the cause of liberation; for if one has the notion that the practice of yoga—the means to true knowledge—is unachievable, one would not engage in those various actions considered causes of liberation. Moreover, death at Mathurā, Kāśī, and so forth cannot possibly be combined. Where the scripture conveys the causality of several factors without any mention of their association (*sāhitya*), there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of rice and barley. Otherwise, the established doctrine of the author of the *Upāya* (Prakāśātmā) would be violated. If that [doctrine] were disregarded, it would follow that even in the case of rice and barley there must be a combination, and it would further follow that sacrifices such as the Vājapeya and Agniṣṭoma would act as mutual auxiliaries.

He does not perceive the five aggregates, nor does he perceive 'five aggregates,' nor does he perceive 'form,' nor does he perceive 'feeling,' nor does he perceive 'perception,' nor does he perceive 'formative predispositions,' nor does he perceive 'consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive 'eye,' nor does he perceive 'form,' nor does he perceive 'eye-consciousness,' nor does he perceive 'contact of the eye,' nor does he perceive 'feeling born of contact of the eye. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive 'ear,' nor does he perceive 'sound,' nor does he perceive 'ear-consciousness,' nor does he perceive 'contact of the ear,' nor does he perceive 'feeling born of contact of the ear. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive 'nose,' nor does he perceive 'odor,' nor does he perceive 'nose-consciousness,' nor does he perceive 'contact of the nose,' nor does he perceive 'feeling born of contact of the nose. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive 'tongue,' nor does he perceive 'taste,' nor does he perceive 'tongue-consciousness,' nor does he perceive 'contact of the tongue,' nor does he perceive 'feeling born of contact of the tongue. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive 'body,' nor does he perceive 'tangible object,' nor does he perceive 'body-consciousness,' nor does he perceive 'contact of the body,' nor does he perceive 'feeling born of contact of the body. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive 'mind,' nor does he perceive 'mental phenomenon,' nor does he perceive 'mind-consciousness,' nor does he perceive 'contact of the mind,' nor does he perceive 'feeling born of contact of the mind.'"

Not so. In every case, the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) alone is the direct cause of liberation. As for death in Kāśī and the like, their status as means to liberation occurs only through the mediation of that knowledge of reality. The meaning of those scriptural passages (*śruti*) which teach that death in Kāśī and so forth are means to liberation is not that they are the *cause* (*kāraṇa*) of liberation, but rather that they are its *instigator* (*prayojaka*). Therefore, even if there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) between knowledge and death in Kāśī by way of the relationship between the mediator and the mediated (*dvāradvāribhāva*), there is no contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "conjunction" applies to cases where multiple causes are taught by the Veda, provided they do not exist simultaneously. Since the knowledge of reality is mental in nature, one can postulate specific classes (*jāti*)—subsumed under the category of "mentality"—that serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of being produced by death in Kāśī; thus, there is no room for mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, since the arising of knowledge cannot occur within the confines of a dead body, the assumption of the acquisition of another body after death in Kāśī is also postulated, as there is no other recourse. As for the instruction of the *Tāraka* mantra by the Lord Mahārudra, this occurs precisely at the stage when one is about to die, because instruction is impossible for one who is already dead. Thus says the Śruti: "For here, when the vital breaths of the creature are departing, Rudra teaches the *Tāraka* Brahman, by which he becomes immortal and attains liberation. This instruction produces the direct realization of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvasākṣātkāra*) through the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), which depends upon the acquisition of another body. One should not object: "If the *Tāraka* instruction occurs at the stage of impending death, the direct realization of the reality of the Self is possible within the confines of that very body; why then assume the acquisition of another body? For if the knowledge of the reality of the Self were accepted as occurring within the confines of that [final] body due to the instruction of the *Tāraka* mantra, then death in Kāśī could not logically be the cause [of liberation]. If it is argued that the intent of the statements teaching death in Kāśī as a cause, as well as the instruction of the *Tāraka* which reveals the name [of the deity], lies solely in their being causes [of liberation] in that manner—otherwise, the fault of one being superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*) relative to the other would be difficult to avoid—then it should be understood that the possibility of the knowledge of reality exists even within the confines of that [final] body.

Death in Kāśī is required for the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) solely through the attainment of the instruction of the *tāraka* [mantra]. And it is only after death in Kāśī that the Lord utters the *tāraka* into the ear. Regarding this utterance, some maintain that even if it does not produce knowledge within the confines of that very body, it produces the knowledge of the reality of the Self within the confines of a body subsequently assumed, by means of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*). Even though death in Kāśī, death in the Gaṅgā, and so forth, may coexist through the medium of an unseen potency, their status as causes is merely optional (*vaikalpika*), according to the reasoning stated above, just like grass and other fuels in relation to fire. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would follow the consequence that death in Kāśī and death in the Gaṅgā—when combined—would fail to produce the result, as is the case with rice and barley. This is because the two cases are dissimilar. To explain: since rice and barley are enjoined in a single context as successive means for accomplishing a sacrifice, once the means has been obtained initially as rice, no further expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) arises for another means. Therefore, the injunction regarding barley must be understood as arising from a primary expectation of an alternative, namely: "If the sacrifice is performed with rice, what is its instrumental cause that makes it a means to the result? Such an expectation has as its object the understanding that the sacrifice is a means to the result when it is qualified by having a cause other than rice, specifically characterized by the absence of rice as its instrument. By supplying the word "or" (*vā*), the sentence "He sacrifices with barley" (*yavair yajati*) must be accepted as producing an understanding of the sacrifice as qualified by both attributes: the absence of rice as the instrument and the presence of barley as the instrument. It is a general rule of the Veda that its purport (*tātparya*) lies in making a subordinate element a necessary factor for that effect which is connected to it as a means. Thus, from the injunction "One should sacrifice with rice," only the sacrifice with rice is understood; and from "with barley," only the sacrifice with barley. Consequently, the attribute of being "with rice" (from the first) is perceived as contributing to the result, and thus neither is non-scriptural. In the present case, however, because the contexts (*prakaraṇa*) are distinct and there is no fixed order of precedence in the application of the injunctions, there arises only the expectation: "What is the means to liberation? Since death in the Gaṅgā, death in Kāśī, and so forth, are enjoined as means to that end, they are understood to be means to liberation precisely when qualified by the absence of association with the others. Therefore, even when death in Kāśī, death in the Gaṅgā, and the remembrance of the Lord Nārāyaṇa are combined, the accomplishment of the result is entirely unimpeded. Unlike the case of rice and barley, where they possess a contradictory nature due to their mutual exclusion, here there is no such thing; rather, there is simply an option between separate alternatives, as in the case of the Vājapeya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. The common saying that "both are non-scriptural" refers to an option consisting of mutually exclusive alternatives. Now, if it is argued that mutual dependence on the absence of the other is unauthoritative in the case of rice and barley—since the initial injunction of rice does not convey that the sacrifice with rice as the instrument is a means to the result when qualified by the absence of barley as the instrument—the answer is no. For although fire is produced from a gemstone independent of grass, one does not say, "Fire is produced from grass or from the gemstone. Furthermore, based on the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that even when the word "or" occurs in a subsequent clause, it conveys the coexistence of the exclusion of the preceding alternative in the latter, just as it conveys the coexistence of the exclusion of the latter in the former, the understanding that rice and so forth are associated with the absence of barley is established by convention in expressions such as "with rice or with barley. Details are found elsewhere.
Thus ends the *Muktivāda* composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya.
